incoherent

in-koh-HEER-unt -- stress on the third syllable, HEER. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Incoherent is expressed in a confusing way.

The letter was so incoherent that the committee could not tell what the writer was actually asking for.

Example

A player runs off the field mid-game shouting something incoherent about a car, a phone, and somebody named Dev, in no order at all. His teammates catch every single word and understand nothing.

Incoherent means the pieces refuse to hold together, so no meaning comes through. It is not about volume or vocabulary -- it is about parts that fail to connect to one another.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disjointed: Disjointed means the connections between the parts are missing: scenes arrive out of order, sentences do not hand off to one another. You can still hear or read each piece clearly. Incoherent is the next stage of the same failure -- the whole no longer makes sense at all, and the listener is lost.

jumbled: Jumbled means shaken out of order, like notecards dropped and gathered up wrong -- the right pieces in the wrong sequence. A jumbled story can often be reassembled. Incoherent is harder to save: its pieces refuse to hold together, so no amount of reshuffling brings the meaning back.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

coherent: clear and logically connected

lucid: clearly expressed and easy to follow

Where it sits · how hard it is to follow — rambling → incoherent → unintelligible

rambling vs. incoherent: Rambling is the gentler fault -- a rambling story wanders, but you can still follow it -- while an incoherent one loses you completely.

unintelligible vs. incoherent: Unintelligible is the end of the road past incoherent: an incoherent answer has parts that do not connect, while an unintelligible one cannot be made out at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin in-)

root — coher-

root — coher-: to stick together (Latin cohaerere 'to cling together,' from co- 'together' + haerere 'to stick')

suffix — -ent

suffix — -ent: doing or being; forms an adjective (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin cohaerere meant 'to stick together,' so with in- ('not') and the adjective suffix -ent, incoherent describes ideas that fail to stick together. Coherent thoughts hold together; incoherent ones fall apart as you speak them.

Use the root in a new word: cohesion

Use the root in a new word: cohesion: Coaches around the league kept praising the young team's cohesion.

Root Check

Word Choice

Incoherent judges speech, writing, and arguments -- an incoherent essay, an incoherent explanation, an incoherent policy. Notice that it can describe either the speaker or the thing said: 'he was incoherent with fever' and 'his answer was incoherent' are both standard.
